title: Why Moderate Democrats Are Magnanimous in Victory
text:
After a pro-oil seminarian from Texas, a pro-gun district attorney from Mississippi, and a “pro-life with a heavy heart” megachurch pastor from Kansas picked up Senate seats for Democrats, you might have expected party centrists to do a fair bit of crowing. Yet many have instead fallen for a new kind of nonbinary politics, one that rejects the division between moderate and progressive. What was once the central fault line of party politics—epitomized by the bitter 2016 presidential primary fight between Bernie Sanders and Hillary Clinton—is now outmoded, prominent moderates are saying.

 “I don’t think of politics on the spectrum of left to right,” Senator Ruben Gallego, a Democrat from Arizona, told me last week at a conference in Denver. He does not care about the ideological valence of policies, he said. “We just care about the results. It’s pretty bad out there.” Instead, Gallego prefers using his own coinage to describe his politics, “big-ass-truck populism”—a program to ensure that everyone who wants a giant vehicle should be rich enough to get it. He espouses Bernie Sanders–style economic ideas (which might formerly have been called progressive), such as raising the minimum wage to $20 and increasing Social Security taxes on high-wage earners. But to actually win votes, Gallego argues, Democrats must not just redistribute; they must also avoid coastal snootiness and off-putting social-justice speak. He was an early critic of the attempted rebranding of Hispanics as “Latinx.” And the big-ass trucks he has in mind are not electric vehicles.

 Gallego was one of several rumored presidential candidates at a gathering this past weekend convened by Majority Democrats, a centrist group that presents itself as an alternative to the “gerontocratic establishment,” the “activist left,” and the MAGA right. Its cardinal virtues are electability and heterodoxy. Many other attendees expected to run in 2028 expressed similar irritation at the labels of “progressive” or “moderate.” Josh Shapiro, the governor of Pennsylvania, declared in his speech that, when it comes to winning over voters, “not one of them gives a damn about shallow litmus tests or where we fall on some imaginary political spectrum.” Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan said that “if you have elected officials who are spending all their time fighting progressive versus moderate, then they have missed the plot of the election.” The real divide, instead, would be between “team fight” and “team flight.” J. B. Pritzker, the Illinois governor, was not at the Denver conference, but he proposed a very similar typology in August : “If there’s a divide in the national Democratic Party that exists, it’s the one between team fight and team cave.”

 [ Read: The rise of the fusion Democrat ] 

 Political binaries are all inexact, but survive because they are useful. Describing politicians as “right” or “left” began during the French Revolution, more than 200 years ago, when monarchists and republicans sat on opposite sides of the National Assembly. The Congressional Progressive Caucus, founded by Sanders, dates back to 1991. These ideological labels will probably not disappear in favor of sorting Democrats as either fighting or feckless. And, as the party decides where it will go in the post-Trump era, such disagreement may actually be generative. “We are about to enter the presidential primary process. And it is good for big, fractious coalitions to have debates, fights, struggles—whatever you want to call it—over our direction,” Matt Bennett of Third Way, a centrist Democratic think tank, told me on Monday.

 The magnanimity that Gallego, Shapiro, and others are showing might be tactical, born of the realization that progressives matter quite a lot in presidential primaries. But the reasons for the détente may also run deeper. Self-identifying as moderate in the face of such immoderate voter anger—about high prices most of all—seems incongruously timid. “I think the party not just accepts, but embraces, the premise that we are in a populist moment,” Jake Auchincloss, a Democratic representative from Massachusetts, told me.

 The party’s answer to economic populism, Auchincloss argued, can go one of two routes: “subsidy populism,” which involves increased government largesse and regulation, and is a recipe for inflation, or “productive populism,” which more lastingly cuts prices by eliminating bureaucracy, local land-use restrictions, and intermediaries in the health-care sector. That debate—between what I would call the “consumer socialist” wing of the party and the “abundance”-minded supply-siders—may well be the defining one of the 2028 presidential primary.

 [ Read: ‘Make politics boring again’ ] 

 If moderates are inching toward progressives on economics—or at least wrapping technocratic reforms in populist packaging—the progressives have lurched toward the moderates on cultural issues, mostly by staying silent. Even if the leftmost Democrats have not entirely abandoned their beliefs, they understand that affordability politics is a better topic of discussion than abolishing prisons and capitalism and making inclusiveness involuntary through DEI policies and pronoun disclosures. “Woke 1 was crazy,” the quote popularized this year by Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, is a neat encapsulation: a half-hearted mea culpa, expressing the desire to move on without too much painful reflection. Some of the worst excesses of that era—calls to defund the police and abolish immigration enforcement, attempts to rebrand mothers as “birthing people”—look unlikely to recur in the 2028 Democratic primary. Class consciousness, once the core of left-wing politics, was strangely absent from the debates over social-justice and identity politics that roiled the party for years; now it is returning to the Democratic Party. Perhaps working-class voters will, too.

 Only a presidential nominee can definitively settle what the post-Trump Democratic Party believes. But that will take longer than a year, and the debate will not be theoretical in the interim. “The candidates who ran for Congress and for the Senate who flipped seats did an incredible job of being very clear in some of the things they wanted to do. And now it’s going to be incumbent upon Democratic leadership to actually do those things,” Abigail Spanberger, the Democratic governor of Virginia, told me. Spanberger, who served in Congress before being elected governor in 2025, advised the new Democratic Congress to industriously pass bills reasserting control over tariffs and the Iran war and rolling back the impending changes to Medicaid that will soon remove millions from the program. Democrats who run states—herself included—must also busy themselves with their own affordability agendas on housing, health care, and energy costs, all while compensating for federal cuts to health-care and food assistance.

 Before the midterms, the jockeying among factions within the party led to discord over how best to challenge Republicans. Spanberger was reluctantly dragged into an effort by her party to redistrict Virginia—an effort that ultimately failed in court. With so much to do now, many in the party think the internecine squabbling should be left behind. “I think that Democrats have just won,” Spanberger said, “so we should shut the fuck up about it, and actually govern.”
